sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A `defer` statement schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function returns. Deferred calls execute in last-in, first-out order.

The deferred function value and arguments are evaluated when the `defer` statement runs, but the call body runs later. A closure may instead read variables when that closure executes.

For example, if a function defers printing `x` as an argument while `x` is one, then changes `x` to two, the deferred call prints one because the argument was captured earlier.

Deferred calls run when their function returns, not at the end of a block or loop iteration. `os.Exit` terminates without running them.

Use defer immediately after acquiring a resource when cleanup must happen on every normal return and panic path, such as closing a file or unlocking a mutex.

sections.title: The core model: defer execution in Go
sections.content:
defer execution in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Defer has two moments. Registration evaluates the function value and ordinary arguments; return executes the saved call. This distinction explains most output questions. Multiple registrations form a stack, so the latest cleanup runs first and can naturally undo nested acquisitions.

sections.content:
The useful question is not whether defer execution in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

Placing `defer resource.Close()` directly after a successful open makes ownership visible. It is especially helpful when later code has several returns. For extremely hot tiny functions, performance can be measured, but correctness and scope should be designed first rather than avoiding defer by habit.

sections.content:
Failures around defer execution in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

A defer inside an outer function's loop does not run after each iteration. Thousands of files can remain open until the whole function exits. Wrapping one iteration in a helper gives each resource its own function scope. Variable capture should be tested with the language's current loop semantics and explicit parameters when clarity matters.

sections.title: The important trade-off: defer execution in Go
sections.content:
defer execution in Go and calling cleanup manually on every return path solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Manual cleanup can happen at an exact earlier point and may be appropriate when resource lifetime must end before more work. Defer is safer across branching paths and panics. A common balance is a small helper whose defer runs promptly at the end of one unit of work.
